prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

MOSCOW, Russia (CNN)  -- Dozens of gay and lesbian rights activists planning a parade in southwestern Moscow Saturday have been detained, Russia's Interfax news agency reported. Gay and lesbian rights activists are detained in Moscow Saturday ahead of a planned march. The arrests included Nikolai Alexeyev, a prominent gay activist in Russia, and his associate Nikolai Bayev, Interfax said, adding that more people trickling into the location were being arrested without explanation. Officials of Moscow's gay community had announced earlier plans to rally at Novopushkinsky Park in central Moscow, Interfax said. The arrests came ahead of Saturday night's Eurovision Song Contest, which is being held in Moscow. The contest has a strong following among the gay and lesbian community.  Watch police break up the march » . Journalists from various countries gathered at the scene, as police barricaded the park with metal bars. Trucks with soldiers onboard were parked on nearby streets, Interfax said. UK gay human rights campaigner Peter Tatchell, in a statement on his Web site ahead of the march, said it was being held to coincide with the final of the Eurovision Song Contest. "This parade is in defense of human rights. We are defending the often violated human rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender Russians. They want legal protection against discrimination and hate crimes. I support their cause. "Not all Russians are homophobic, but many are. Gay Russians suffer queer-bashing attacks, blackmail, verbal abuse and discrimination in education, housing and employment. This shames the great Russian nation." The Eurovision Song Contest, which began in 1956, sees singers and groups from a short list of European nations perform a specially written song before telephone votes from each nation decide the winner. In western Europe, the contest is regard as a light entertainment spectacular, with a strong following among the gay and lesbian community. Many fans dress up, hold parties and gather round the TV to watch the three-hour-plus televised marathon. In recent years, however, eastern European nations, which take the contest much more seriously, have come to dominate. The contest is also known for its political edge, as nations either give zero points to traditional enemies -- or, if they are enjoying good relations, the maximum number of points, as a sign of friendship. The most famous winners of the contest were ABBA, who came to attention as the Swedish entry with "Waterloo" in 1974. In 1988, Celine Dion won the contest while singing on behalf of Switzerland. The dance show Riverdance first came to attention as an interval act when the contest was held in Dublin, Ireland, in 1994. The organizers of the contest estimate it is watched by 100 million people worldwide.

Officers moved in shortly after activists gathered near Moscow State University, arresting participants and forcing others away from the area. Among those detained were prominent Russian campaigner Nikolai Alexeyev and British activist Peter Tatchell.

# LGBT activists arrested in Moscow hours before Eurovision final

**MOSCOW, May 16, 2009** — Russian police detained prominent LGBT rights campaigners Nikolai Alexeyev, Nikolai Bayev and British activist Peter Tatchell on Saturday as they attempted to hold a banned demonstration in Moscow, hours before the city hosted the final of the Eurovision Song Contest.

The protest, organized under the banner of “Slavic Pride,” was intended to draw international attention to discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people in Russia and neighboring countries. Activists deliberately scheduled it for the day of the Eurovision final, when Moscow was crowded with foreign journalists, performers and visitors.

Police moved in shortly after campaigners gathered near Moscow State University. Officers seized banners, pushed demonstrators toward waiting vehicles and detained several dozen people, including Russian, Belarusian and foreign activists. Counterprotesters were also reported at the scene.

Alexeyev — also widely transliterated as Nikolai Alekseev — was one of the principal organizers of Moscow’s repeated attempts to stage a Pride march. Bayev was another leading Russian campaigner involved in the action. Tatchell, a veteran British human-rights activist, said police treated demonstrators roughly and accused the authorities of suppressing a peaceful call for equality.

The activists had sought permission to hold a march and rally, but Moscow officials prohibited the events. The city had banned previous Pride demonstrations, and Mayor Yuri Luzhkov had repeatedly denounced gay parades, at one point describing them as “satanic.”

Organizers said their demands included freedom of assembly, equal legal treatment and an end to official hostility toward LGBT people. Although consensual same-sex relations had been decriminalized in Russia in 1993, activists said discrimination and violence remained widespread and that authorities routinely prevented them from demonstrating publicly.

The arrests underscored a contrast between Eurovision’s image as a colorful, inclusive international celebration and the policies of its host city. The contest has long attracted a substantial LGBT following, although the European Broadcasting Union, which oversees Eurovision, presents it as a nonpolitical entertainment event.

## Why Eurovision was in Moscow

Moscow hosted the 2009 Eurovision Song Contest after Russian singer Dima Bilan won the previous year’s competition in Belgrade with “Believe.” Under Eurovision tradition, the winning country receives the right to stage the following year’s event.

The semifinals took place on May 12 and May 14 at Moscow’s Olimpiysky Arena, with the grand final scheduled for the evening of May 16. The production was one of the most elaborate in the contest’s history and was seen by Russian officials as an opportunity to present a modern, internationally confident image of the country.

Norwegian singer Alexander Rybak ultimately won the final with “Fairytale,” receiving what was then a record points total.

For LGBT campaigners, Eurovision’s global audience offered a rare opportunity to challenge that carefully managed image. Alexeyev and fellow organizers argued that international visitors should be made aware that Moscow’s authorities would celebrate Eurovision’s flamboyant culture while refusing LGBT Russians permission to assemble peacefully.

Most of those detained were later released, but the police action became one of the most prominent human-rights controversies surrounding the 2009 contest. It also foreshadowed a broader tightening of restrictions on LGBT expression in Russia, culminating several years later in the federal law banning the dissemination of so-called “propaganda of non-traditional sexual relations” to minors.

## Dozens of LGBTQ activists detained in Moscow, Interfax reports

**MOSCOW —** Russian police detained dozens of gay and lesbian rights activists attempting to hold a demonstration in Moscow, the Interfax news agency reported.

The gathering was organized to draw international attention to restrictions on LGBTQ rights while Moscow was hosting the Eurovision Song Contest. Authorities had refused permission for the demonstration, and officers moved rapidly to break it up.

Interfax reported that protesters and several foreign supporters were among those taken into custody. Activists said the action was peaceful and accused officials of using Eurovision’s global profile while silencing calls for equal rights. Police maintained that the demonstrators had participated in an unauthorized event.

The detentions highlighted the contrast between Eurovision’s image as a celebration of diversity and the Russian government’s treatment of LGBTQ activism. The song contest has a particularly large queer following, and rainbow flags are a familiar sight among its audiences.

## Why Eurovision is so popular

The **Eurovision Song Contest** is one of the world’s largest live entertainment broadcasts. Organized by the **European Broadcasting Union**, it brings together public broadcasters from Europe and some neighboring or affiliated countries. Australia has also competed since 2015.

Its popularity comes from a distinctive mixture of:

- Live music and elaborate stage productions  
- National rivalry and audience participation  
- Camp humor, fashion and spectacle  
- Voting drama, with points awarded by national juries and viewers  
- A sense of shared international celebration  

Recent editions have typically attracted a global television audience of well over 150 million people, though totals vary from year to year.

## A brief history

Eurovision began in **1956**, partly as an experiment in linking European countries through new live-broadcast technology after World War II. The first contest was held in Lugano, Switzerland, with seven participating nations.

The competition expanded steadily. Each country generally submits one original song, performed live during televised semifinals and a grand final. The winning country traditionally hosts the following year, although financial, security or political circumstances can require another broadcaster to step in.

The familiar phrase **“douze points” — “12 points”** comes from the contest’s scoring system, under which countries award their highest score to a favorite entry.

## Is Eurovision political?

Eurovision’s rules describe it as a **nonpolitical event**, and overt political messages are prohibited. In practice, however, politics has always surrounded the competition.

Voting patterns can reflect geography, migration and cultural ties. Governments use hosting duties as a form of soft power, while performers and audiences sometimes turn songs, costumes or gestures into statements about war, identity, democracy or human rights.

Examples include Ukraine’s politically resonant victories, debates over Israel’s participation, disputes involving Russia, and recurring controversies over flags and lyrics. Russia was excluded from the contest after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Eurovision also has a strong association with LGBTQ visibility. Performers such as **Dana International** and **Conchita Wurst** became international symbols, making clashes over queer rights especially conspicuous when the contest is staged in socially conservative countries.

## Famous winners

Among Eurovision’s best-known champions are:

- **ABBA** — Sweden, 1974, with “Waterloo,” which launched the group internationally  
- **Céline Dion** — Switzerland, 1988, with “Ne partez pas sans moi”  
- **Johnny Logan** — Ireland’s two-time winning performer, in 1980 and 1987  
- **Dana International** — Israel, 1998, with “Diva”  
- **Lordi** — Finland, 2006, with the hard-rock anthem “Hard Rock Hallelujah”  
- **Conchita Wurst** — Austria, 2014, with “Rise Like a Phoenix”  
- **Loreen** — Sweden, winner in 2012 and 2023, becoming the first woman to win twice  
- **Måneskin** — Italy, 2021, with “Zitti e buoni,” followed by major international success  
- **Nemo** — Switzerland, 2024, with “The Code,” becoming the contest’s first openly nonbinary winner  

Eurovision’s enduring appeal lies in that tension: it presents itself as light entertainment beyond politics, yet repeatedly becomes a stage on which Europe’s cultural and political arguments are played out before a vast audience.

**Russian police break up LGBT rights rally ahead of Eurovision final**

**MOSCOW, May 16, 2009** — Russian riot police broke up an LGBT human-rights demonstration in Moscow on Saturday, detaining campaigners only hours before the city hosted the final of the Eurovision Song Contest.

The protest, organized by Russian activists as part of a “Slavic Pride” initiative, had been banned by Moscow authorities. Participants nevertheless gathered near Moscow State University to demand equal rights for lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people and to condemn official restrictions on peaceful assembly.

Police moved in almost immediately, seizing banners and forcing protesters into waiting vehicles. Among those detained were leading Russian activist Nikolai Alexeyev and veteran British campaigner Peter Tatchell. Journalists at the scene reported that officers dragged some demonstrators away as they attempted to speak to television cameras.

“This is a fundamental human right. We are not going to be intimidated by the Russian authorities,” Tatchell told reporters before being arrested.

As police pulled him toward a vehicle, he shouted: “This shows the Russian people are not free.”

Organizers said dozens of people were detained, including Russian activists and supporters from Belarus and other countries. Police also held several opponents of the rally after confrontations near the protest site. Most detainees were later released, although some faced allegations connected to participation in an unauthorized demonstration.

Moscow officials had repeatedly refused permission for gay-pride events in previous years, citing security concerns and public opposition. Activists argued that the bans violated Russia’s constitutional guarantees of free expression and assembly, as well as its obligations under the European Convention on Human Rights.

The timing of Saturday’s protest was intended to draw international attention to the treatment of LGBT people in Russia while Moscow hosted Eurovision, one of the world’s most-watched entertainment broadcasts. The contest has a large LGBT following, and campaigners accused organizers and visiting delegations of failing to challenge the city’s prohibition of the demonstration.

Tatchell said the police action was incompatible with the inclusive image promoted by Eurovision. “The arrest of peaceful protesters is an attack on the whole Eurovision ethos of international friendship and understanding,” he said in comments released by his campaign.

Russian authorities defended the intervention on the grounds that the gathering had not been authorized. Under Russian regulations, public demonstrations generally required prior official approval, and police routinely dispersed events held after municipal authorities rejected organizers’ applications.

The rally began with only a small group of participants, reflecting the expectation of a swift police response. Activists carried flags and attempted to display slogans calling for equality before officers closed in. The operation unfolded in front of a large contingent of Russian and foreign media, giving the demonstration substantially greater visibility than its size might otherwise have attracted.

Eurovision organizers sought to keep the dispute separate from the competition. The European Broadcasting Union, which oversees the song contest, said Eurovision was a non-political event, while human-rights groups countered that the detention of peaceful campaigners could not be dismissed as unrelated to the festivities.

The crackdown underscored the increasingly difficult environment facing Russia’s LGBT community. Pride organizers in Moscow had been denied permission to march each year since 2006, and previous attempts to demonstrate had ended in arrests and attacks by nationalist and religious opponents.

Saturday evening’s Eurovision final proceeded at Moscow’s Olimpiisky arena under heavy security. Norway’s Alexander Rybak won the contest with the song **“Fairytale.”** Outside the celebration, however, the images of police detaining LGBT campaigners offered a stark contrast to Eurovision’s message of unity across national and cultural borders.
